description: We are a team passionate about science and technology. Our name, Bosón de Quásar, reflects our mission: to combine the power of the fundamental (boson) with the astonishing and energetic (quasar) to create innovative solutions that inspire and enable informed decision-making.
summary:
ALBA (Autonomous Lunar Basin & Horizon Analyzer) is an interactive web application designed to evaluate and compare lunar landing sites and mission dates—with a specialized focus on the Moon’s South Pole. Planning missions like NASA’s CLPS and Artemis requires balancing solar power availability and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication in extreme terrain where small shifts in coordinates or launch dates can plunge a lander into days of shadow or radio blackout.

ALBA bridges the gap between raw scientific data and agile decision-making by combining JPL DE421 ephemeris and NASA LOLA digital elevation models into one intuitive workspace. Users can select curated sites or custom coordinates, scrub across mission timelines, compare multiple site-date scenarios side by side, and switch seamlessly between a 2D Horizon Panorama, a 3D Orbital Globe, an Immersive 3D Lunar Surface & Descent Simulator (including a first-person spacecraft view up to the zenith), and an Operational Metrics Dashboard to immediately identify viable mission windows.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

ALBA evaluates whether a lunar landing site and mission window are operationally viable by computing the exact topocentric positions of the Sun and Earth against the real surrounding lunar terrain:

  1. High-Precision Ephemeris & Libration (MOON_ME frame): The backend computes time-series positions of the Sun and Earth using Skyfield and NASA JPL DE421 kernels (de421.bsp) paired with high-precision lunar orientation data (moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc). Working in the Moon Mean Earth / Polar Axis (MOON_ME) frame naturally accounts for the Moon’s orbital variations and Earth’s optical libration (the apparent wobble of Earth in the lunar sky).
  2. Real Topographic Horizon & Local DEM Raycasting: Using NASA LOLA South Pole stereographic elevation data (ldem_80s_20m, 20 m/pixel), ALBA casts 360° rays from the observer’s elevation (accounting for lunar curvature drop and zero atmospheric refraction) to extract the real mountain/crater silhouette and a local 16 km × 16 km elevation grid around the landing target.
  3. Power & Communication Window Analysis: At each timestamp, ALBA compares the Sun’s and Earth’s elevation angles against the local terrain horizon to determine line-of-sight visibility, solar elevation angle, normalized solar power index (sin⁡(elevation)\sin(\text{elevation})sin(elevation)), Earth communication windows, joint operational windows (simultaneous sunlight + Earth link), and time remaining until sunset or Earthset.

How is the project creative? (4-in-1 Visualization Engine)

Instead of forcing users to interpret raw tables or static plots, ALBA synchronizes four interactive views around a live timeline controller:

  • 2D Topocentric Sky Panorama: Plots the 360° LOLA horizon mask alongside the full trajectories of the Sun and Earth, highlighting terrain occlusion events.
  • 3D Orbital Space View: Renders the Moon using NASA SVS 4720 (CGI Moon Kit) LROC WAC color and LOLA bump maps aligned to MOON_ME, showing the real-time solar terminator, the landing beacon, local tangent plane, and 3D direction vectors to the Sun and Earth.
  • Immersive 3D Surface & Descent Simulator: Reconstructs the 16 km × 16 km LOLA terrain patch (128×128 mesh with regolith micro-relief) surrounded by the 360° horizon massif. Users can watch a CLPS/Artemis-style lander descend from 5,000 m to touchdown while its solar array and high-gain antenna actively track the Sun and Earth. It features three camera modes: 3rd-Person Orbit (with terrain collision clamping so the camera never clips underground), Descent View, and 1st-Person Spacecraft POV (Cabina 1ª), which lets users look from the lander’s deck all the way up to the zenith (+90∘+90^\circ+90∘) to verify overhead passes.
  • Operational Metrics & Multi-Scenario Comparator: Summarizes sunlight %, Earth visibility %, joint viability %, peak/mean solar angle, and allows side-by-side comparison of alternative sites and dates when schedules shift.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Drastically reduces the time needed to re-evaluate landing sites or launch slips from hours of multi-tool cross-referencing (JPL Horizons, QuickMap, Moon Trek) to seconds in a single interface.
  • For Science Teams & Educators: Makes the counterintuitive physics of the Lunar South Pole—such as grazing sunlight, multi-kilometer crater shadows, Peaks of Eternal Light, and Earth hovering near the horizon in a 14-day libration loop—immediately visual and intuitive.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Skyfield, JPL SPICE Kernels (de421.bsp, moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc), NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, NASA LOLA GeoTIFF DEM (ldem_80s_20m).
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Three.js (WebGL 3D orbital and surface engines), Tailwind CSS, NASA SVS 4720 CGI Moon Kit textures.

Factors Considered

  • Airless Body Physics: Zero atmospheric refraction; sharp shadow transitions determined strictly by local LOLA topography and spherical horizon drop.
  • Performance & Accessibility: Async progressive texture loading (~556 KB static NASA maps with instant procedural fallback) and GPU resource disposal keep load times fast while serving both technical planners and the general public.
